video_title: Annie Lowrey on the Time Tax, Fraud, and Rationing by Paperwork
transcript: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome  back to Conversations with Tyler. Today,   I’m very happy to be chatting with  Annie Lowrey. She has a new book out,   new and excellent book called The Time Tax:  How the Government Wastes Our Time—and How to   Fix It. The government does not just waste your  money. Annie is a staff writer at The Atlantic.   She has worked in the past and written for New  York Times, Slate.com, and many other outlets.   She also has an earlier book, Give People Money,  on universal basic income. Annie, welcome. ANNIE LOWREY: Thank you. COWEN: Could you start by giving us a single clear  example of your main thesis about The Time Tax? LOWREY: Absolutely. In most of our peer  countries, so wealthy countries, democratic   countries with decent public administration,  you do not have to do your own taxes. In Japan,   if you earn a salary, you do not have to do  anything. You do not have to engage in the   tax process at all. In many other countries,  they pre-fill your tax forms, send them to   you. You can make a correction if desired or  if necessary. The tax authority does much of   the work for you. We could do this. Nine in 10  American households take the standard deduction   and have fairly simple tax situations. We do not  do this. The IRS is legally not allowed to do it. COWEN: If you had to pick a  part of government, taxes aside,   where in general these obstacles and time  taxes are the worst, what else would you name? LOWREY: The single worst program in my mind is  TANF, which is cash welfare and a lot of other   things. This is the program that hypothetically  is supposed to address child poverty. It does   not change the child poverty rate. It is  enormously onerous and punitive to comply   with. It’s a terrible waste of the $16.5 billion a  year associated with it. Just in general, I would   say safety net programs are not great. Programs  that are mostly used by higher-income Americans   are much, much, much better. The safety  net, and specifically welfare, is the worst. COWEN: As you know, under  Biden, for a brief while,   we had a child tax credit. It seemed to me  from a distance pretty clean and simple. Yet   it was not greatly loved. What is your  read of the political economy of that? LOWREY: I think that there is a tension with all  submerged benefits. They work much better. They’re   easier for the government to administer. They have  higher participation or take-up rates because most   people do file a tax return. It’s fairly unusual  not to. Even very, very low income, because below   a certain level, you’re not actually required  to file federal taxes. That’s pretty uncommon. They work better. The problem with them is,  and I look to Suzanne Mettler’s work on this,   is that people don’t know that they are receiving  benefits. These programs are not visible. They’re   not understood by the recipients. You could  look at the CTC. I remember I went reporting   about it. People had no idea what it was  even when they were getting the money.   I think that there’s ways to get around that.  You could send checks. The IRS could send checks   with the program name on it instead of direct  deposit. That’s a little bit less elegant too. COWEN: If you had to pick an area of government  that works pretty well, US government,   and does not have such a big time tax overall,  what would you point to as us getting it right? LOWREY: The postal service and Social Security’s  retirement programs. Those are both pretty good.   Social Security also has other  programs, SSI, which is mostly   used by very, very low-income seniors with  disabilities or who are blind. Disability   insurance is run by the Social Security  Administration. The retirement program,   it’s less than 1 percent overhead. It’s  great. It does all the work for you. COWEN: Isn’t our whole postal service  a time tax in the aggregate? Denmark,   just this year, abolished its postal  service. They don’t have any. Now,   I understand we’re not in a position to  do exactly the same, but shouldn’t we be   moving away from postal service, basically  zeroing it out over the next 10 years? LOWREY: Did they make it so that it’s  all digital? Did they digitize things? COWEN: Well, I don’t know who the “they”  is. Direct mail there has gone away. LOWREY: Oh, yes, that’s interesting. I don’t know.  I think in a high inequality country such as ours,   where you still have a lot of people who don’t  have smartphones and don’t have computers,   that’s why I would be very concerned  about the postal service going away. COWEN: That’s why we need 10 years. You want to  tax people, tax in the broad sense of the term,   living in rural areas, if only because it’s  much harder to have government help them, right? LOWREY: Yes. COWEN: If rural areas don’t get mail  anymore, maybe that’s a good thing. LOWREY: I don’t think that that’s a good  thing for the people in the rural areas,   though. There’s always going to be people  in rural areas. As a general point, do you   want the government to be encouraging  people to not live in rural areas? COWEN: Absolutely, that’s me. Welcome to the show. LOWREY: That’s feels very  nanny state-ish of you, Tyler. COWEN: I don’t want to subsidize rural areas,   and we do it in so many ways,  including with our farm programs. LOWREY: We do. We really, really absolutely do. COWEN: It gets harder to help people with  government. There’s a lot more market power   in rural areas, like how many supermarkets are  there, how many hospitals, probably just one,   if that. Let’s get everyone into the  suburbs, or heaven forbid, the cities. LOWREY: I can’t imagine a  less popular policy than that. COWEN: Absolutely. LOWREY: All of our policies are aimed at allowing  people to be in place. We’re very stuck as people.   We don’t move in the way that we used to. You  can never suggest that we should just depopulate   places. If you’re running for president,  Tyler, I don’t think you’re going to win. COWEN: Now let’s think about our  COVID experience. In a number of ways,   we relaxed controls on benefits. LOWREY: We did. COWEN: It became much easier to get unemployment   insurance. Interviews were just  hard to pull off flat out, right? LOWREY: Yes. COWEN: It seems that fraud  went up a lot. In net terms,   maybe we need the time taxes and the other  nonsense just to prevent what happens when   we take them away. We tried that in  2020, 2021, it didn’t go that well. LOWREY: I do not think that time taxes,  administrative burdens, having more of them,   would have prevented the fraud at all. This was,  in part, because we didn’t have these programs set   up. There were two things that they were taking  advantage of. A lot of it was criminal groups,   criminal actors. One was the aid to  small businesses. They were setting   up sham small businesses and getting checks.  That was legitimately a really big problem. Again, the book is about people, so I  would separate that. I didn’t get into   business regulation. This is entirely  about individual citizens. Then in UI,   this was really bad. This was a catastrophe.  The problem is, even going into the pandemic,   every single recession that we have, we have this  conversation about how stupid it is that we have   these ancient infrastructures, literally,  programs running on COBOL, and that states   don’t have the right incentive to upgrade  service delivery and their digital systems. If you’re a governor and you have a low  unemployment rate, what governor is going   to devote a huge amount of money to upgrading a  state UI system? Some states have gotten better   systems since, but broadly, no. They’re just as  bad. Then the next time the next recession comes,   we’ll have the exact same conversation over  again. I think that the government actually   having more state capacity and more agile digital  systems would help with fraud prevention. I do not   think that putting more work on individuals  is going to reduce the amount of fraud. COWEN: Let me give you another example: Medicare.  It’s a big chunk of the federal budget, right? LOWREY: Huge, yes. COWEN: It seems to me they cover too many medical  procedures. You’re going to have knee surgery.   You can just get it covered. Wouldn’t it be  better if you had to go through a big time   tax to get your knee surgery covered than just  indiscriminately having Medicare pick up the bill? LOWREY: No. COWEN: Why not? LOWREY: There are many other ways to reduce  medical spending, and I really do think that   we should look at those ways. There’s no  more popular policy proposal out there for   both Democrats and Republicans than having  the government do price controls in more   pharmaceuticals. That would really, really help  with medical spending. I do not think making it   onerous to get your knee repaired is a good use of  anybody’s time. It is not a way to ration medical   care. It’s not fair. It shouldn’t be that  if you are going to get your knee repaired,   it’s because you have Medicare and are good  at paperwork. It’s not a nice way to ration. COWEN: Even if we want to do these other  policies to lower costs, there’s way too   many knee surgeries. A lot of them don’t work.  There’s also a problem with back surgeries.   Shouldn’t we just be tougher and force people  to go through more hoops? I know it’s not nice,   but most ways of saving money are not nice.  If it’s not an effective medical procedure,   let’s be much tougher. Maybe not cover  it at all. Just give people some cash. LOWREY: Why not lower the payment rate? COWEN: Absolutely. Make it like Medicaid. LOWREY: Make it so that it’s not profitable  for doctors to perform in that case. There’s   got to be other ways to do it. You could tax  things that you can produce more of. More work,   more income, more natural resources.  You can’t give people more time. I   think it should be a really serious  thing to take it away from them.   I just think that there’s a lot of policy options  to accomplish the goal that you’re describing,   and I see the addition of paperwork as being a  particularly illegitimate way to go about it. COWEN: Let’s consider another example. Medicaid  fraud in Minnesota over Somali autism claims. I’m   not sure it’s a lot of money. I know  it’s debated. I looked into it. It’s   probably not a lot of money, but it became a big  headline, and people claim it’s a lot of money.   They feel outraged. There’s an immigration  issue, maybe there’s a race issue, there’s an   autism issue. The result is that it turns into  a big thing, and it makes policy much worse,   it makes discourse much worse, but there was  clearly some fraud. Would we not have been   better off with more procedures to limit Somali  autism claim fraud through Medicaid just to   protect the rest of the integrity of the systems?  Now it seems like the whole system is fraudulent. LOWREY: I think that public confidence in  programs is very, very important. I think   that reducing fraud is part of that. I think  if we had simpler systems that the government   was better at administering, we would have less  fraud and people would feel more supportive of   the government. I also think that we have a huge  problem with trust because the government is so   ineffective and treats the time of citizens as  valueless. I think that we’re lacking confidence   in public systems for that reason also, and  politicians don’t always take that seriously. I saw this quite vividly in San  Francisco where I lived for many years,   that the state was so incompetent at doing  anything, the San Francisco government—a lot   of this came up in terms of building and  housing policy, that there was just like   a pox on everybody’s house attitude.  I think that that’s a problem, too. I do note that in Medicare and Medicaid,  the problem with fraud is almost all on   the provider side. It’s nursing homes that are  defrauding the government. It’s doctors’ offices,   it’s hospital systems that are defrauding the  government. Individual fraud can only be so   bad. There’s only so much money that you’re  going to get from the government for claims   or whatever else it is. To do big fraud, you have  to be doing a lot of processing. I would actually   love to reduce overhead in other programs  so that we can focus on the criminal groups   and organizations and legitimate providers  that are engaging in fraudulent activity. COWEN: Voters often seem more outraged by  individual fraud, even though it costs less.   There were actual Somalians who showed up and  said, “My kid has autism,” when the kid probably   didn’t have autism. Then people end up turning  against immigration, or immigration of Somalians. LOWREY: Sure. COWEN: For that reason, don’t we need to really be   pretty strict with the individuals  because that’s what bugs voters? LOWREY: I think that reducing incidents of  fraud is a good and important thing to do.   I’m not pro-fraud. I wouldn’t make a pro-fraud  argument. However, I think that there are ways   to do it that don’t require inconveniencing  everyone and the 99.9 percent of people who   are not engaging in fraud. I do think that  fraud has also been a way of making these   programs seem illegitimate so that voters will  tolerate cutting them even if voters might want   us to have more progressivity or the current  level of progressivity in the current system. COWEN: Maybe this is impossible to do, but  in the aggregate, if you had to estimate,   how much time does the time  tax cost us, say per person,   how many minutes or hours in a  day, what’s your best estimate? LOWREY: The best estimate I have come up with  comes from the American Time Use Survey. The   problem with the American Time Use Survey when  it comes to measuring what people are doing   is that it’s very ineffective at measuring  time use when you are doing many things at   once. If you are waiting on hold on the  telephone while you’re cooking dinner,   you’re only doing one thing. It might say  that you’re cooking or you’re taking care   of your kids. The other thing is, the time tax  is in all kinds of little different categories,   and so it’s not agglomerated. If you’re  looking at what I think of as roughly   as bureaucratic time total spent,  it’s 50 hours per person per year. COWEN: It’s close to an hour a week? LOWREY: Yes, something like that. Some people it’s   way more, some people it’s way less.  There’s a lot of inequality in it. COWEN: I would think it’s higher than  that, but obviously you’ve studied this. LOWREY: Again, I don’t think that  ATUS is picking up a lot of data.   The other issue is that OIRA does  not measure this functionally at all. COWEN: What best predicts the inequality? Who  are the groups that pay the highest time taxes? LOWREY: People with involvement with the criminal  justice system, immigrants, and poor people. COWEN: Of the wealthy, which are the wealthy  who pay the highest time taxes? They may pay it   indirectly. Their subordinates have to do things,  but they have to pay the subordinates more, right? LOWREY: Yes. They vault over them. I think a lot  of it is subordination. It’s really interesting   to see the places where the wealthy have to use  the same services or have to pay the same time   taxes as lower income people. The one that I think  bizarrely has no care for whether you’re wealthy   or poor is something like permitting to renovate  your house. Even very, very wealthy people in San   Francisco will wait 500 days for a permit,  going through many rounds of public comment. Low-income San Franciscans are not renovating  their homes, they’re very unlikely to own them,   and probably don’t have the money for renovation.   That’s one where I think something like taxes,  high-income people obviously are much, much,   much, much, much more likely to itemize, so  their tax process is going to be much longer,   but they’re also much more likely to use a  high-priced accountant, something like that. COWEN: They’re still paying the tax.  They have to pay for the accountant. LOWREY: Yes, they’re paying the accountant. COWEN: Now, you mentioned something like an  hour a week, say it’s somewhat more than that,   but how much of that time do you think  people really don’t mind that much? LOWREY: Sort of in the same  way that people enjoy errands. COWEN: Yes. I go shopping when I could  just order from Amazon. And I enjoy the   shopping—I’m not sure I enjoy it;  but I don’t stop doing it either. LOWREY: I don’t know anybody who likes  this stuff. I know a handful of people,   I should say, who like this stuff. I think  that some people like doing their own taxes.   I’m sure you know people who act as a  VITA, like a volunteer tax preparer,   but a lot of this is just quite miserable  and pointless. I don’t think that there are   necessarily people who find it rewarding.  There’s always somebody, but I don’t know. COWEN: Putting aside the extreme cases  like, oh, you’re sent to jail, or, oh,   you’re kicked out of the country, but of  tasks that you do and finish and complete,   which is psychologically the most tortuous in your  view? Like, I hate filling out visa applications,   because I always have these photos, and  I have to shrink them down to a smaller   JPEG size and then upload it to a  website, and I’m terrible at that. LOWREY: Do you mean for me personally? COWEN: For you and then just overall. LOWREY: For me personally, the great irony is that  I am terrible at all of these bureaucratic things,   and I am married to a person who has  a very different brain and is very   on top of them and manages basically  all of the personal administration,   the household administration. I didn’t go  to the dentist for 20 years, not because I   have something against dentistry, but  just because it wasn’t front of mind. I’m currently having an issue where when I moved  from California to New York, I didn’t get a New   York driver’s license, but now I’ve lost my  California license, and it appears to be that   the only way to get a driver’s license and thus to  be able to rent a rental car is for me to go get   a learner’s permit from the state of New York, and  I have to go to driving school. I have to take the   test, the written and the test, but I don’t have a  car, so I’m going to have to borrow a car to take   the driving test because I can’t rent one. Anyway.  All of them. I am bad at absolutely all of them. Also, I have a rare degenerative disease  which requires a lot of documentation and   managing of medical stuff. I had to trigger  my short-term disability policy. That took   forever. I needed The Atlantic to give me  a second computer, which they wanted to do,   so I simply had to get a letter from  a doctor. It took forever. I hate all   of this. This is the stuff that I  personally struggle with the most. In terms of the burdens that the  government is putting on other people,   the psychologically torturous stuff is really,  really bad. On many assistance applications,   there are detailed questions about your height  and your weight, which can be painful for some   people. Questions about the paternity of your  children, where your children were conceived,   what day they were conceived. That’s the  stuff that I think it’s the government   saying that it doesn’t care about you. That  it wants it to be painful. It’s really,   really invasive and really upsetting. Child  support, as a general point, I agree with it   in concept, but as actually administered can  be really painful for people to deal with. COWEN: Let’s say we’re comparing with  the private sector. Now, say, medicine,   it’s half public-funded, give or take.  That’s a joint public-private sector. LOWREY: I consider it public, just given  how heavily regulated it is and how big   the government is. I have private insurance,  but the government is setting the rules there. COWEN: Something that is more or less pure private  sector, where is the worst time tax both for you,   and you think in the aggregate? Amazon  is a tiny time tax. You fill it out,   you click, the package comes.  It’s great. Where is it bad? LOWREY: I think that there’s nothing like the  health system in terms of just the bureaucratic   morass. I think as a general point, businesses  have every incentive to reduce time taxes for   people who are consuming things and to increase  them as much as they are legally allowed to and   as much as is practical for people who are trying  to stop spending, which I think you can see. A   lot of businesses don’t do it because it’s bad  for business for people to hate your business.   They’re cross-pressured in that way. I think that  there’s nothing like healthcare and associated,   like getting your parents into a skilled nursing  facility type thing—it’s absolutely miserable. COWEN: This is a small thing, but it bugs me  all the time. I’m on a purely private sector   website. I can’t blame the government at  all, and it turns out I already have an   account at the website. I try to register  as a guest, and it’s never that simple. LOWREY: No. COWEN: Why does this go wrong? Why is  this not fixed in a world with AI agents? LOWREY: I’m convinced that white-collar  technology, labor-saving stuff,   I’m convinced it’s all Jevons paradoxical.  I think that basically anything that is   designed like email to make your life easier  will at some point make it worse. We’ve made   it so that it just multiplies the number  of tasks. The things that companies can   do to you multiplies. I do not want to use  passkeys. It feels like private companies are   just hell-bent on—I don’t want to know what  a passkey is—getting you to use them. It’s   absolutely nutty. The password managers, but then  you have to manage the manager. It’s all a lot. COWEN: If I travel to Harvard and  maybe I bought a plane ticket for   $400 and I can get reimbursement,  that is hell. That’s one of the   worst private sector experiences I have  is learning a new software system to be   reimbursed for a small sum of money and  having to go through a whole rigmarole. LOWREY: Yes, exactly. There’s some amount that   you just won’t do it because you value  your own time and your blood pressure,   right? It’s absolutely annoying. There  were these rules that used to make airlines   reimburse you if they bounced you off a plane.  That’s gone. Anything having to do with airlines,   and they’re like, “We’ve severely inconvenienced  you, so we’ve given you some miles,” or some   credit or something. This is the first book: Give  People Money. Give them cash. They like that. COWEN: Now, government, virtually  by definition, operates at scale,   unless it’s, say, a small town. How long will  it be before AI agents are just built to do   almost all of this for us? You just say to your  agent, “Hey, fill out these benefits form,” and   then you go away, you go to sleep and it’s  done? Won’t that happen within five years? LOWREY: I imagine so. The questions that I  have are, one, are the lower-income people,   who are the users of the most burdensome programs,   do they know about those agents? Do they  feel comfortable using them? I don’t know. COWEN: Not now— LOWREY: Not now. COWEN: —but, say, within five years— LOWREY: Yes, definitely. COWEN: —if it’s just a pure gain. LOWREY: The second thing is that a lot of it is  not really paperwork. It’s mandatory interviews,   it’s urine screens, it’s collecting  data that might be hard to collect,   and answering questions that an AI agent might  not be able to answer for you. For instance,   unlike other programs, jobless benefits are given  to the individual. It’s state and individual. SNAP benefits depend on your  household. You, in some cases,   will have to say how you split up the cost  of staples with the people in your house.   It’s really hard because the government doesn’t  have a stable definition of what a household is,   and it could be very hard to say who is in your  household and how you’re splitting things up. I   think that AI will help with a lot of this. I was  skeptical, but the best civic technologist I know   thinks that it’ll help a lot—and he’s a guy who’s  been in the muck of this for a really long time,   and knows the technology part of it—he’s  convinced that AI will help. I don’t know. COWEN: The AI can interview you and say, “Well,  please tell me these things. I’m going to need it   to answer the questions for your SNAP benefit.”  You intermediate through the AI, which is nicer,   friendlier, easier to deal with, and then it  deals with the nasty person in the government. LOWREY: Yes, and very often, the government  will ask you a question in a way that some   lawyer wrote in some very legalistic fashion. I  think the AI is unusually good at saying, “Oh,   this is what they’re actually asking, and this is  what the general advice is for how to do that.” COWEN: Now, very big picture question.  Fertility rates are low in the US,   lower elsewhere. They’re not going to pop up  anytime very soon. The future of this country,   it really depends on the quality of immigrants  we attract. If we have a welfare system where   it’s really hard to get benefits, don’t we, in  fact, attract a higher quality of immigrant,   more ambitious people and more self-sustaining,  than if benefits are just easy to get? Isn’t the   significance of that really quite large in  a future where native fertility is so low? LOWREY: Why do you think it is that if  we have such a clunky system now we’ve   managed to attract such a good  quality of immigrants thus far? COWEN: Because people who want to come  just to get the benefits might say, “Oh,   in Europe, they’ll just hand me the money, give  me the free apartment, put me up in the hotel.” LOWREY: I see what you mean. COWEN: You come to the US, it’s a huge  pain. Maybe there’s a wisdom in that. LOWREY: Yes, and you can come. My  understanding was that the welfare   magnet hypothesis didn’t pan out. It makes  some sense, but I think that the issue is,   can you actually get here and come  here is a big problem. Then you’re   barred from accessing the safety net  as an immigrant for long periods of it. COWEN: Part. Much of it, yes. Not all of it. LOWREY: Yes, not all of it. Your children,  especially if they’re born here, they have   access, so there’s that. In general, I  think the policies work well when they   have a direct goal rather than relying  on indirect mechanisms like these. If we   want to attract more and better immigrants,  why don’t we just create policies that will   get them to come here. Like, if you get your  PhD here, you automatically get a Green Card,   that kind of thing. I think that that would  lead a lot of immigrants to come back. COWEN: The current system, it selects for  people having stamina, conscientiousness,   focus, drive, willing to put up with  indignities, and smart enough to get   through the systems that may not be in  their language. You could argue what   we have is those policies. I know plenty of  lazy PhDs. Most PhDs are lazy, I would say. LOWREY: Really? COWEN: I don’t want that to  be the standard. Of course,   they are. It’s become negative  selection, relative to IQ. LOWREY: Huh. You’re looking for  entrepreneurial people with a   lot of get-up-and-go, people who can make  it through the maze that we have set up. COWEN: More O-1s, and then somewhat reform H-1B,   and to have more of them, and  none of these crazy $100,000 fees. LOWREY: If you’re thinking that the  H-1B and the O-1 is working well,   why not just make those much,  much, much bigger programs? COWEN: Oh, of course, but keep the benefits  tough and stingy, or, in some cases, impossible,   which is not a time tax. If you know you  can’t get it, you don’t bother to apply,   but it’s like a time tax in the sense  that it keeps you away from the benefit. LOWREY: Right. I just don’t think that you  should be creating chaos and taking people’s   time by making the actual administrative part  of it difficult. I think there’s always many   other ways to get the policy outcome that  you are searching for than larding the   government up. It means that the government  is wasting more money. Your overhead cost   is going to be higher. I know that immigration is  self-financing because we are applying these fees,   but nevertheless, I just think that  there’s better ways to go about it. COWEN: Here’s a question from a reader,  which I’m paraphrasing: “Do you favor much   easier access to benefits, but randomized  harsh, credible punishments for offenders?   So you audit one in every 100, every 1,000  applications. If the person did something wrong,   you come down on them really hard. The time  tax mostly vanishes, but there’s still this   somewhat arbitrary punishment meted out  to some of the people who are frauds.” LOWREY: I think you have to separate  out the issue of improper payments   from purposeful fraud. Improper payments are  a function of the complexity of this system.   If the system were easier and the rules were more  straightforward, and you weren’t asking people   who don’t own a computer for their monthly gross  income and also their net income over the past   six months, and that’s really hard to do, and  a million other little questions, the improper   payment rate would go down if the government were  doing more work and the rules were simpler. You   would also have lower bureaucratic costs. Yes, I  absolutely support making the rules much simpler. And maybe that means that you have to adjust  the benefit threshold. Meaning that you get it,   and then auditing on the back end. I don’t  know that I think that you have to have   obscenely harsh punishment, though.  Why do you need the harsh punishment   as opposed to the auditing and the threat  of that and the threat of civil penalties? COWEN: If you only audit one  in 5,000, people will think,   “Oh, I can get away with it.” The punishment  needs to really be harsh to scare them off. LOWREY: Yes. I think you could just do more  reasonable audits. I don’t necessarily think   that you need to have extremely harsh punishments  for this kind of thing. Also, for fraud, intent   is important, to show that they intended; they  knew that they didn’t have access to the benefit,   they knew that they put the wrong paperwork  in there. As a general point, I think that the   benefit fraud rate is quite low. I’m not concerned  that we’re losing too much money to fraud. COWEN: Now, from 1990 to 2014, the number of  people on disability insurance increased by   about four times. Even though jobs got safer,  the number of people killed by their job went   down steadily. Does that not mean that  disability insurance should just be much   tougher to get? More bureaucracy, more  standards, more process, more whatever. LOWREY: Yes. I think that there were some reasons  that more Americans became disabled. Population   aging is one, the general rise of chronic health  conditions related to obesity is another. And   so I think that we should be somewhat more  neutral in saying, “Is it people defrauding   the system just because that number has gone up  so much?” I don’t think so. I don’t think so. Disability is extraordinarily onerous to apply for  and has very, very stringent fraud checks already.   In 5 percent of applications, the applicant  submits more than 1,000 pages of medical   paperwork. It’s a lot. 11,000 Americans die  waiting on a disability determination each year.   Yes, the caseload has gone up,  but recently it’s been going down,   so I don’t think that we’re worrying that it’s  just going up and up and up and up and up and up. COWEN: Yes, it’s gone down a lot since 2014. LOWREY: Gone down a lot, right? COWEN: The job market got better, is part of it. LOWREY: I worry that we are giving benefits  to people who are not disabled and do not need   them. I also worry that we are denying  benefits to people who actually do,   so I don’t know that I see a strong case for  making disability much more burdensome as opposed   to looking for other ways to help the system.  Disability, I do think that it’s a program that   is extremely important. It is the only  long-term help for people who are impaired   in their ability to work, but it’s an extremely  burdensome program for the government to manage,   so I don’t know that I see the case for  adding paperwork to it at this juncture. COWEN: If I look at governments where  processes seem pretty straightforward,   they very often seem to have smaller  populations, say, below 20 million. Now,   I’m not sure what is causing what here, but what  do you think is the exact reason why a small   population is correlated with better processes?  Is it less federalism? Is it somehow the smaller   number of people; they feel more cooperative, or  is it something else? Do you have a view on that? LOWREY: Yes, I think it’s, in some cases,  federalism. I think it’s homogeneity.   Finland, it’s basically mostly ethnically Finnish  people. The United States is quite unusual in our   ethnic and racial diversity. I think when you’re  thinking about small nations, they tend to be   fairly racially, ethnically homogeneous. It feels  like there’s higher social trust. Functionally,   everybody is related to one another. That’s  really not true in the United States. COWEN: Should the US have less federalism? LOWREY: Yes. COWEN: I’m not saying it’s practical  in the sense of getting support,   but some way you could bring that about? LOWREY: Absolutely. COWEN: What would it be? LOWREY: I think that there is the case for local  control of certain things; some things: policing,   sewers. Makes sense, right? We need to do that  locally. I think that for the administration of   mass programs, if it is legally possible  to have the federal government do it,   the federal government should be doing it.  For one, people move from state to state   and locality to locality constantly. It makes  sense if you have a jobless insurance program   or similar to administer it. There’s  just the simple multiplicity effect. We have more than 100 TANF programs. We have  56 Medicaid programs. In terms of overhead,   it just makes sense to have one. The  federal government doesn’t have a   balanced budget rule. They, every year now,  spend more than they take in tax revenue,   and I think that generally, federal programs are  better managed. Not always, but generally, yes. COWEN: Should Brooklyn be a separate  city from the rest of New York? LOWREY: No, but I don’t know about Staten Island. COWEN: It’s big, right? I was  just going to ask about Staten   Island. New Jersey is clamoring for it, right? LOWREY: I think so. I guess that the people  of Staten Island should self-determine. COWEN: What do you think they would do? LOWREY: I don’t know. I don’t know. Actually,   I need to go over there and do some  surveying and knocking on doors. COWEN: I haven’t been there in 20 years. Is  there Sri Lankan food? Is that the reason to go? LOWREY: Yes, Sri Lankan food. I took the ferry.  The ferry costs $0. You go there and back,   and it’s a perfect happy hour, so I did that  recently. The time I was there, before that,   I’ve not spent a lot of time on Staten Island.  I was reporting there a couple of years ago,   but look, I don’t have strong views on Staten  Island. I think it’s great. I also feel like I   haven’t been in New York for long enough; I’m  not a New Yorker; I can’t set policy for New   York. Brooklyn feels like it should be part  of New York to me, now living in Brooklyn. COWEN: There’s a theme recurring  through your book in a number of   different places that it’s too hard to vote. LOWREY: Yes. COWEN: Now, I’m of the view that  it should not be that easy to vote,   at least in the United States. What exactly is  the gain we get from having more people vote?   Given that, for instance, people didn’t  even know what the child tax credit was,   even if they were receiving it.  Don’t we just get better outcomes if,   say, only half the people vote, which of  course will skew toward the more educated? LOWREY: I don’t think so. COWEN: Why not? LOWREY: I think that democracy is important for   reasons of principle that are  more important than policies. COWEN: I’m all for democracy, right? There’s  no country where you can vote by just leaning   back on your sofa and screaming out whom  you favor. There’s some cost. You can set   the cost where you want. Americans today seem  fine with the costs being higher than in many   places. You make the costs lower, you get inferior  outcomes, including on the issues you care about. LOWREY: I don’t know that I think  that that’s true. Do we know that? COWEN: Maybe “no” is too strong a word,  but we know that more educated people   make better voting choices than  less educated people on average. LOWREY: I think my view is  only principled. I don’t   care about outcomes. I think if you’re a  democracy, people should be able to vote. COWEN: Oh, sure, they should  be able to, but how easily? LOWREY: As easily as possible. COWEN: You would, even in countries  with high voter participation rates,   subsidize voting, give everyone a  free ride, do whatever was necessary? LOWREY: Yes, I think so. I think when  you look at countries with very high   voter participation rates, do you think  that they have worse outcomes, or do you   just think that their polities are different  such that you end up with different policies? COWEN: The latter. LOWREY: Voting is compulsory in some places. COWEN: They tend to be better educated  at the lower end, for one thing. LOWREY: Right. Then I think, again, you  want to do more education. You want to   make it easier for people to go to school. You  don’t want to make it hard for them to vote. COWEN: I’m all for making school easier. Now, you  have an earlier book called Give People Money,   which is basically pro-UBI, to oversimplify a bit. LOWREY: Indeed. COWEN: There have been UBI  studies since then. How does   your current view differ from your earlier view? LOWREY: I think that the studies have been  sobering, and, yes, I have updated my priors,   and I think that some of the ancillary benefits  that I thought we could see through cash haven’t   materialized, and I take that seriously. I think  that there is still a case for doing it, because   the point of giving people money is to merely  give them money so that they can buy things,   and I think that the case for that remains. I  think it is noncorrupted, that their lives don’t   improve as much as I would have thought, I think,  isn’t necessarily a case against the policy. COWEN: There’s an argument that your earlier  argument is stronger than you thought. Say AI   truly is a big deal, and we all live to 100,  but day-to-day, we’re not really happier,   per se, because of AI. This, to me, is one  plausible scenario. I’m not sure it will happen,   but it could happen. Then the purpose  of UBI is not to make people happier,   but just to stop them from being  less happy due to instability. LOWREY: Yes. COWEN: The only benchmark is, can  UBI keep people where they were at,   on some dimensions, and they still get to  live to 100, which of course they want,   and then overall, it’s just a  way of making the system stable? LOWREY: Yes, absolutely. When I wrote the  prior book, the AIs that were out were garbage,   and it was really not clear that they would  ever get to the place that people said that   they would get. I remember even when I  first moved out to the Bay Area in 2018,   you would talk to people who did AI work and  they seemed like religious zealots in some ways. COWEN: Seemed like? LOWREY: Yes, they’d be like, “No, I  promise it’s going to change everything;   I’ve seen inside the machine.”  I’d be like, “Okay, buddy. Sure,   great. The computer’s not really better,  and they aren’t really getting better,   and this is a time of really remarkably  little technological progress.” I was   very wrong about that and really found ChatGPT  remarkable when I got access to it, and I do. I was extremely dismissive at the time of the  notion that AIs would necessitate UBI. I don’t   know that I would go so far as to say that  I think that we’ll need a UBI because of AI,   but I certainly think that we should  be starting to think about that kind of   policy if the improvements that we’re seeing  continue forward, and if there is a lot of   pressure on the white-collar workforce, which  I think we won’t know for a couple of years. Yes, I think that if we see a situation  in which GDP is radically increasing,   productivity is increasing, and unemployment  is going up, that would be very strange,   and I think we would have to start  looking at UBI-type functions. COWEN: Are raccoons evolving into pets? LOWREY: No, they are not. COWEN: Should they? LOWREY: No. COWEN: Should more things be  pets, or fewer things be pets? LOWREY: Fewer things. COWEN: No tigers? LOWREY: No, I don’t think that you should be  able to have a nondomesticated animal as a   pet. This is one of my strongest-held  and probably least popular positions,   and that means that I do not think that you should  be able to have sugar gliders. I do not think you   should be able to have most types of fish. I  don’t think you should be able to keep birds. COWEN: That would be federal or local governments  doing that? Getting back to our earlier question. LOWREY: Federal. COWEN: Federal? LOWREY: Nondomesticated birds, I should  say. You can have chickens. Chickens   are domesticated, but tropical birds, I  don’t think you should be able to keep. COWEN: Why are you visiting Namibia? LOWREY: Ah, the Namib Desert. I’m very, very  excited to see petroglyphs. As a general point,   I organize a lot of my travel around  deserts and moss, to see those,   so I’m very, very excited. I’m very excited  for dark skies. I’ve been to South Africa,   but I haven’t traveled extensively in that region. COWEN: You said moss, M-O-S-S? LOWREY: Moss. COWEN: Where is the best place  in the world to go see moss? LOWREY: The Pacific Northwest, I think, is the  best moss that I have seen in the United States.   My understanding is that there are places in  Japan that have extraordinary moss. I have   only ever been to Tokyo. Have you been to mossy  places in Japan? You’re better traveled than I am. COWEN: I think in retrospect, they seemed mossy,  but I wasn’t very aware of it at the time. LOWREY: You’re not a moss traveler.  Have you been to the Sundarbans? I   don’t know how to say that. The  mangrove forest in Bangladesh? COWEN: No, never been to Bangladesh  at all, I’m sorry to say. LOWREY: I haven’t either,  and I very much want to go. COWEN: Why do you like architectural brutalism? LOWREY: Oh, I just find it visually  interesting and beautiful. I like to   feel tiny in front of buildings, and I like the  idea of creating warm spaces within imposing   structures that make you feel uncomfortable.  It’s like the jolie laide of architecture. COWEN: My favorite brutalism is in former   communist countries. Do you  have a favorite brutalism? LOWREY: Boston City Hall. It’s really ugly. COWEN: Why are tattoos so popular  now, including with women? LOWREY: For the same reason  we scribble on cave walls. COWEN: One of those is your body, and  it’s still somewhat hard to reverse,   right? It can take 12 sessions  to get it off, and it hurts. LOWREY: Yes, it’s reversible. I actually  think that the capacity to remove tattoos,   while wonderful for some people who have a tattoo  that is prohibiting them from getting employment,   reminding them of something painful, or, goodness  forbid, if you have hate speech or similar on your   body, I think it’s good that you can take the  tattoo off, but in general, I think that the   idea of having and then removing tattoos is  not good for tattoo culture. I have tattoos,   and I think that they’re a really nice reminder  of time and place. They’re permanent ephemera. COWEN: You recently read a book called A  History of Christianity. Which one was it,   and what was interesting in the book to you? LOWREY: This was A History of Christianity:  The First Three Thousand Years.   One of the things that really stuck with  me was that I, despite being Catholic,   had not entirely internalized that  Christians start off as a strange,   tiny Jewish sect of people that are found to  be often mentally unstable and deeply annoying. COWEN: This book communicates that? LOWREY: Indeed, that Judaism is not the  predominant mode of worship or culture   at the time, and Christianity, which then  comes to dominate so much of the globe,   starts off as an offshoot of that; of  people who are insisting that they are   seeing apparitions and people walking through  walls. It was a very, very, very good book. COWEN: How essential do you view  Christianity to Western liberalism? LOWREY: When you say “essential,” do you mean  “positive,” or do you just mean “influential”? COWEN: Influential but positive: the notion that  Jesus Christ was an individual. It’s a story very   different from “might makes right.” We valorize  the victim. It easily translates into talk of   individual rights and liberties and constitutional  procedures, at least that has been argued. LOWREY: Yes, I agree with that, but  I certainly don’t see Christianity as   essential to enlightenment or good governance  in any way, shape, or form. I do think that   it had that effect, but I don’t think that  it would be necessary in some other world. COWEN: Not that many Christian  countries have achieved the same, right?   You could say Japan has for a while. LOWREY: Yes, I was going to say Japan. COWEN: Yes, that’s one. LOWREY: South Korea? COWEN: South Korea’s pretty Christian in terms  of actual belief. I’m not sure of the numbers. LOWREY: Did it inform the  structure of government, though? COWEN: I don’t know. LOWREY: I don’t know. That’s an actual question;   I don’t know enough about it. I’ve been to  South Korea, but I don’t know that much. COWEN: Other than Japan, I see very few examples. LOWREY: Yes. I don’t know. I would  have to think about it more. Also,   there’s so much Christianity; it gets so  everywhere-d that I don’t know. I’m not sure. COWEN: I tend to worry quite a bit, now  that we are genuinely less Christian,   that this will hurt the chances  of liberalism in our future. LOWREY: I think that that might be right. I’m  not saying, when I’m talking about the church,   the political actor “the church,” which  obviously has a very checkered history,   but I do think that it was good that you had an  institution that was so predominant in people’s   lives, reminding them of the importance of  sin and of being a person of integrity and   caring for the neighbor. Although,  then again, the world, as it’s become   less Christian, it’s become safer, more  redistributive, so I’m not really sure. COWEN: What do you think of Ross Douthat’s  famous comment? It’s something like, “Well,   if you don’t like the Christian right, wait till   you see the post-Christian right,”  which he said some while ago, right? LOWREY: Yes. I think that’s completely accurate,   and I think that our most notable Christians  are not particularly Christian right now. Again,   as a Catholic, the notion of being yelled  at specifically by two successive popes,   as J. D. Vance has been, it’s tough  to imagine that. It’d be very painful. COWEN: Other than facts about moss, what  is it you think you learn when you travel? LOWREY: Oh, goodness. In some ways, I feel  like the emergence of a global monoculture,   this idea of it, I do think  that shows up especially in   urban places. I think that it is really,  really important to recognize your own   privilege and to see how other people live. I  think it’s important in the sense of trusting   that people know what they value and value  very, very, very different things than you do. It slows time down, which is a big thing for  me. The time I spend traveling seems to go   20 times as slowly as an average  day in the office, and I really,   really like that telescoping effect, and I  look for nondrug ways for that to happen. COWEN: Could you name a city that  you feel more or less successfully   rebels against the global monoculture,  but it’s not just a complete wreck?   You could say Lagos, but Lagos is  a complete wreck. A well-run city   that avoids the traps of many places, where  every coffee shop looks the same or whatever. LOWREY: That’s a great question. A lot of  the traveling I do is for outdoors stuff,   and I do think that the global monoculture  and Instagram has been very terrible for that,   for opening beautiful places up to people who just  want to take photographs and leave. It’s really,   really awful. There, I understand it’s the “you’re  not in traffic, you are traffic” phenomenon,   but I really mean people who are desecrating  these places that are very fragile ecosystems   and where you do want to meter access, and  you do want people to, for instance, take   out their trash and understand what to do if you  encounter a wild animal and that kind of thing. In terms of a city that feels  really, really wildly different,   I just think that there’s lots of  places I go that there’s no tourists,   and they’re wonderful for that. When I  report, even more so than being a tourist,   being a reporter is the best way to find  someplace because I’m always amazed by how   much people will tell you about their lives  and show you about their lives. You really   get to see life on the edge of Lake Victoria  or very close to the India-Bangladesh border. Similarly, going to weddings abroad is  another way to do that, if you ever get   invited to a wedding. One of my favorite  weddings that I went to was in Pakistan,   which I never would have gone to  Pakistan, I think, without that,   or maybe I would have. It was a perfect  way to get a glimpse of Pakistani society. COWEN: That, for me, is a case where  the private sector time tax is too high. LOWREY: Yes. Oh, wow. COWEN: If it were a half-day wedding, I would  go, but a three-day wedding in South Asia,   I’d just feel, no, I’ll be wanting to check  my email the whole time, and that’s rude. LOWREY: Oh, yes. No, no. They really, really do  weddings well. I would also note that Pakistan,   I believe, has much heavier time taxes than we  do. There’s a lot of interesting thinking about   postcolonial states and paperwork burdens.   There’s a good book that I read about  Pakistan that I forget the exact title,   but it was about Pakistan’s issues with paperwork  and the transition from British rule to self-rule. COWEN: Should friendships have  explicit time taxes? For instance,   people from the Soviet Union, they often expect  their friends to pick them up from the airport— LOWREY: Oh, I love that. Yes. COWEN: —even though that’s not a thing anymore.  You can just Uber, taxi. It doesn’t matter if   your income is high enough. It’s expected that  someone goes to pick you up. Is that good/bad? LOWREY: Yes, there’s no inconvenience in  friendship if the point is to do things   and spend time together. I note that I think the  best way to make friends is not to make yourself   available for what other people need but to  ask for help. I remember one escalation of a   friendship that happened to me recently: My older  son had had a dental procedure in the morning,   and I needed to pick my younger son up  from school. My husband wasn’t around,   and no childcare was around, and my mom couldn’t  make it. The older son needed an adult to be with   him, and I couldn’t leave him alone, so I asked a  friend to come over and sit with this kid who had   just been given a large dose of ketamine for  20 minutes. I had a bunch of people say yes,   and one friend came over and sat with my son  in bed and looked at her phone for 20 minutes.   There is no inconvenience in friendship. People  like to be asked to do things, too, I think. COWEN: That’s useful, right?  Say it’s not really useful,   that it’s just an ongoing act of  signaling to show you’re a true friend. LOWREY: Oh, absolutely. Definitely.  It’s because I think that the point   is to spend time, certainly. Do you find  that there are social conventions that   you despise having to comply with in  your life but still have to do it? COWEN: I don’t know. I don’t think I ever despise,   but there are various slight annoyances,  or I wish things were more efficient. LOWREY: Yes. The one that I really struggle  with is that I have email and text and WhatsApp   and Signal and lots of other modes—Instagram  messages. I really, really despise having to   keep up with people on all of those forms  of communication. I think of texting as   being fundamentally asynchronous, and that you  shouldn’t have to socially respond to a text. I only like socializing in person; I want to see  people, I want to be visually with them. I hate   all of the digital upkeep, and I’m really,  really bad at it, and it’s known among my   friends that I’m bad at this. Even my husband  is like, “You’re a terrible texter, and you’re   mean over text.” I’m like, “Well, I’m not trying  to be mean.” I text like a boomer, apparently. COWEN: My slight gripe is there’s too  many networks, so I feel there should   be email and one system of texting. There’s  Signal, there’s WhatsApp, there’s iMessenger. LOWREY: It’s too much. COWEN: There’s other stuff.  There’s Twitter Direct Message. LOWREY: Awful. I don’t do social media anymore,  so I don’t do Twitter anymore at all. I have   an Instagram account that I’m not on very  often. I don’t Facebook, I don’t Bluesky,   and I really appreciate the time that I’ve  gotten back from that. Particularly X, I think,   is a terrible mode of discourse, and I think  that it rewards unseemly emotions in people. COWEN: Just to finish up with the last  question, I ask this of many of the guests,   but first, to mention your book  again, Annie Lowrey, The Time Tax:   How the Government Wastes Our Time—and How to  Fix It. What is it you wish to learn about next? LOWREY: Oh, actually, I just got  two books about the Mexica people,   the Aztecs. I’d like to read those books and  then go see Aztec artifacts and structures. COWEN: That’s a [Inga] Clendinnen book? A  lot of people have been reading that lately. LOWREY: Yes, that was how I saw it. It was a  lot of people were reading it. Now I’m like,   “Who was it who recommended it?” I had  wanted to do more travel in Mexico,   so I got Fifth Sun, and then just  Aztecs, I think, is the other one,   which I’m excited to read. Actually, from  your podcast, I got the book on Vermeer,   which I’m excited—I know nothing about  him, and I’m very excited to read that. COWEN: Great. Annie Lowrey, thank you very much. LOWREY: Thank you.

transcript_segments.text: TYLER COWEN: Hello, everyone, and welcome  back to Conversations with Tyler. Today,
I’m very happy to be chatting with  Annie Lowrey. She has a new book out,
new and excellent book called The Time Tax:  How the Government Wastes Our Time—and How to
Fix It. The government does not just waste your  money. Annie is a staff writer at The Atlantic.
She has worked in the past and written for New  York Times, Slate.com, and many other outlets.
She also has an earlier book, Give People Money,  on universal basic income. Annie, welcome.
ANNIE LOWREY: Thank you.
COWEN: Could you start by giving us a single clear  example of your main thesis about The Time Tax?
LOWREY: Absolutely. In most of our peer  countries, so wealthy countries, democratic
countries with decent public administration,  you do not have to do your own taxes. In Japan,
if you earn a salary, you do not have to do  anything. You do not have to engage in the
tax process at all. In many other countries,  they pre-fill your tax forms, send them to
you. You can make a correction if desired or  if necessary. The tax authority does much of
the work for you. We could do this. Nine in 10  American households take the standard deduction
and have fairly simple tax situations. We do not  do this. The IRS is legally not allowed to do it.
COWEN: If you had to pick a  part of government, taxes aside,
where in general these obstacles and time  taxes are the worst, what else would you name?
LOWREY: The single worst program in my mind is  TANF, which is cash welfare and a lot of other
things. This is the program that hypothetically  is supposed to address child poverty. It does
not change the child poverty rate. It is  enormously onerous and punitive to comply
with. It’s a terrible waste of the $16.5 billion a  year associated with it. Just in general, I would
say safety net programs are not great. Programs  that are mostly used by higher-income Americans
are much, much, much better. The safety  net, and specifically welfare, is the worst.
COWEN: As you know, under  Biden, for a brief while,
we had a child tax credit. It seemed to me  from a distance pretty clean and simple. Yet
it was not greatly loved. What is your  read of the political economy of that?
LOWREY: I think that there is a tension with all  submerged benefits. They work much better. They’re
easier for the government to administer. They have  higher participation or take-up rates because most
people do file a tax return. It’s fairly unusual  not to. Even very, very low income, because below
a certain level, you’re not actually required  to file federal taxes. That’s pretty uncommon.
They work better. The problem with them is,  and I look to Suzanne Mettler’s work on this,
is that people don’t know that they are receiving  benefits. These programs are not visible. They’re
not understood by the recipients. You could  look at the CTC. I remember I went reporting
about it. People had no idea what it was  even when they were getting the money.
I think that there’s ways to get around that.  You could send checks. The IRS could send checks
with the program name on it instead of direct  deposit. That’s a little bit less elegant too.
COWEN: If you had to pick an area of government  that works pretty well, US government,
and does not have such a big time tax overall,  what would you point to as us getting it right?
LOWREY: The postal service and Social Security’s  retirement programs. Those are both pretty good.
Social Security also has other  programs, SSI, which is mostly
used by very, very low-income seniors with  disabilities or who are blind. Disability
insurance is run by the Social Security  Administration. The retirement program,
it’s less than 1 percent overhead. It’s  great. It does all the work for you.
COWEN: Isn’t our whole postal service  a time tax in the aggregate? Denmark,
just this year, abolished its postal  service. They don’t have any. Now,
I understand we’re not in a position to  do exactly the same, but shouldn’t we be
moving away from postal service, basically  zeroing it out over the next 10 years?
LOWREY: Did they make it so that it’s  all digital? Did they digitize things?
COWEN: Well, I don’t know who the “they”  is. Direct mail there has gone away.
LOWREY: Oh, yes, that’s interesting. I don’t know.  I think in a high inequality country such as ours,
where you still have a lot of people who don’t  have smartphones and don’t have computers,
that’s why I would be very concerned  about the postal service going away.
COWEN: That’s why we need 10 years. You want to  tax people, tax in the broad sense of the term,
living in rural areas, if only because it’s  much harder to have government help them, right?
LOWREY: Yes.
COWEN: If rural areas don’t get mail  anymore, maybe that’s a good thing.
LOWREY: I don’t think that that’s a good  thing for the people in the rural areas,
though. There’s always going to be people  in rural areas. As a general point, do you
want the government to be encouraging  people to not live in rural areas?
COWEN: Absolutely, that’s me. Welcome to the show.
LOWREY: That’s feels very  nanny state-ish of you, Tyler.
COWEN: I don’t want to subsidize rural areas,
and we do it in so many ways,  including with our farm programs.
LOWREY: We do. We really, really absolutely do.
COWEN: It gets harder to help people with  government. There’s a lot more market power

LOWREY: We did.
COWEN: It became much easier to get unemployment

LOWREY: Yes.
COWEN: It seems that fraud  went up a lot. In net terms,

COWEN: Let me give you another example: Medicare.  It’s a big chunk of the federal budget, right?
LOWREY: Huge, yes.
COWEN: It seems to me they cover too many medical  procedures. You’re going to have knee surgery.

tax to get your knee surgery covered than just  indiscriminately having Medicare pick up the bill?
LOWREY: No.
COWEN: Why not?
LOWREY: There are many other ways to reduce  medical spending, and I really do think that

COWEN: Even if we want to do these other  policies to lower costs, there’s way too

but most ways of saving money are not nice.  If it’s not an effective medical procedure,

LOWREY: Why not lower the payment rate?
COWEN: Absolutely. Make it like Medicaid.
LOWREY: Make it so that it’s not profitable  for doctors to perform in that case. There’s

COWEN: Let’s consider another example. Medicaid  fraud in Minnesota over Somali autism claims. I’m
not sure it’s a lot of money. I know  it’s debated. I looked into it. It’s

LOWREY: I think that public confidence in  programs is very, very important. I think

I saw this quite vividly in San  Francisco where I lived for many years,
that the state was so incompetent at doing  anything, the San Francisco government—a lot
of this came up in terms of building and  housing policy, that there was just like
a pox on everybody’s house attitude.  I think that that’s a problem, too.
I do note that in Medicare and Medicaid,  the problem with fraud is almost all on

or whatever else it is. To do big fraud, you have  to be doing a lot of processing. I would actually
love to reduce overhead in other programs  so that we can focus on the criminal groups
and organizations and legitimate providers  that are engaging in fraudulent activity.
COWEN: Voters often seem more outraged by  individual fraud, even though it costs less.
There were actual Somalians who showed up and  said, “My kid has autism,” when the kid probably
didn’t have autism. Then people end up turning  against immigration, or immigration of Somalians.
LOWREY: Sure.
COWEN: For that reason, don’t we need to really be
pretty strict with the individuals  because that’s what bugs voters?
LOWREY: I think that reducing incidents of  fraud is a good and important thing to do.
I’m not pro-fraud. I wouldn’t make a pro-fraud  argument. However, I think that there are ways
to do it that don’t require inconveniencing  everyone and the 99.9 percent of people who

programs seem illegitimate so that voters will  tolerate cutting them even if voters might want
us to have more progressivity or the current  level of progressivity in the current system.
COWEN: Maybe this is impossible to do, but  in the aggregate, if you had to estimate,
how much time does the time  tax cost us, say per person,
how many minutes or hours in a  day, what’s your best estimate?
LOWREY: The best estimate I have come up with  comes from the American Time Use Survey. The
problem with the American Time Use Survey when  it comes to measuring what people are doing
is that it’s very ineffective at measuring  time use when you are doing many things at
once. If you are waiting on hold on the  telephone while you’re cooking dinner,
you’re only doing one thing. It might say  that you’re cooking or you’re taking care
of your kids. The other thing is, the time tax  is in all kinds of little different categories,
and so it’s not agglomerated. If you’re  looking at what I think of as roughly
as bureaucratic time total spent,  it’s 50 hours per person per year.
COWEN: It’s close to an hour a week?
LOWREY: Yes, something like that. Some people it’s
way more, some people it’s way less.  There’s a lot of inequality in it.
COWEN: I would think it’s higher than  that, but obviously you’ve studied this.
LOWREY: Again, I don’t think that  ATUS is picking up a lot of data.
The other issue is that OIRA does  not measure this functionally at all.
COWEN: What best predicts the inequality? Who  are the groups that pay the highest time taxes?
LOWREY: People with involvement with the criminal  justice system, immigrants, and poor people.
COWEN: Of the wealthy, which are the wealthy  who pay the highest time taxes? They may pay it
indirectly. Their subordinates have to do things,  but they have to pay the subordinates more, right?
LOWREY: Yes. They vault over them. I think a lot  of it is subordination. It’s really interesting
to see the places where the wealthy have to use  the same services or have to pay the same time
taxes as lower income people. The one that I think  bizarrely has no care for whether you’re wealthy
or poor is something like permitting to renovate  your house. Even very, very wealthy people in San
Francisco will wait 500 days for a permit,  going through many rounds of public comment.
Low-income San Franciscans are not renovating  their homes, they’re very unlikely to own them,
and probably don’t have the money for renovation.
That’s one where I think something like taxes,  high-income people obviously are much, much,
much, much, much more likely to itemize, so  their tax process is going to be much longer,
but they’re also much more likely to use a  high-priced accountant, something like that.
COWEN: They’re still paying the tax.  They have to pay for the accountant.
LOWREY: Yes, they’re paying the accountant.
COWEN: Now, you mentioned something like an  hour a week, say it’s somewhat more than that,
but how much of that time do you think  people really don’t mind that much?
LOWREY: Sort of in the same  way that people enjoy errands.
COWEN: Yes. I go shopping when I could  just order from Amazon. And I enjoy the
shopping—I’m not sure I enjoy it;  but I don’t stop doing it either.
LOWREY: I don’t know anybody who likes  this stuff. I know a handful of people,
I should say, who like this stuff. I think  that some people like doing their own taxes.
I’m sure you know people who act as a  VITA, like a volunteer tax preparer,
but a lot of this is just quite miserable  and pointless. I don’t think that there are
necessarily people who find it rewarding.  There’s always somebody, but I don’t know.
COWEN: Putting aside the extreme cases  like, oh, you’re sent to jail, or, oh,
you’re kicked out of the country, but of  tasks that you do and finish and complete,
which is psychologically the most tortuous in your  view? Like, I hate filling out visa applications,
because I always have these photos, and  I have to shrink them down to a smaller
JPEG size and then upload it to a  website, and I’m terrible at that.
LOWREY: Do you mean for me personally?
COWEN: For you and then just overall.
LOWREY: For me personally, the great irony is that  I am terrible at all of these bureaucratic things,
and I am married to a person who has  a very different brain and is very
on top of them and manages basically  all of the personal administration,
the household administration. I didn’t go  to the dentist for 20 years, not because I
have something against dentistry, but  just because it wasn’t front of mind.
I’m currently having an issue where when I moved  from California to New York, I didn’t get a New
York driver’s license, but now I’ve lost my  California license, and it appears to be that
the only way to get a driver’s license and thus to  be able to rent a rental car is for me to go get
a learner’s permit from the state of New York, and  I have to go to driving school. I have to take the
test, the written and the test, but I don’t have a  car, so I’m going to have to borrow a car to take
the driving test because I can’t rent one. Anyway.  All of them. I am bad at absolutely all of them.
Also, I have a rare degenerative disease  which requires a lot of documentation and
managing of medical stuff. I had to trigger  my short-term disability policy. That took
forever. I needed The Atlantic to give me  a second computer, which they wanted to do,
so I simply had to get a letter from  a doctor. It took forever. I hate all
of this. This is the stuff that I  personally struggle with the most.
In terms of the burdens that the  government is putting on other people,
the psychologically torturous stuff is really,  really bad. On many assistance applications,
there are detailed questions about your height  and your weight, which can be painful for some
people. Questions about the paternity of your  children, where your children were conceived,
what day they were conceived. That’s the  stuff that I think it’s the government
saying that it doesn’t care about you. That  it wants it to be painful. It’s really,
really invasive and really upsetting. Child  support, as a general point, I agree with it
in concept, but as actually administered can  be really painful for people to deal with.
COWEN: Let’s say we’re comparing with  the private sector. Now, say, medicine,
it’s half public-funded, give or take.  That’s a joint public-private sector.
LOWREY: I consider it public, just given  how heavily regulated it is and how big
the government is. I have private insurance,  but the government is setting the rules there.
COWEN: Something that is more or less pure private  sector, where is the worst time tax both for you,
and you think in the aggregate? Amazon  is a tiny time tax. You fill it out,
you click, the package comes.  It’s great. Where is it bad?
LOWREY: I think that there’s nothing like the  health system in terms of just the bureaucratic
morass. I think as a general point, businesses  have every incentive to reduce time taxes for
people who are consuming things and to increase  them as much as they are legally allowed to and
as much as is practical for people who are trying  to stop spending, which I think you can see. A
lot of businesses don’t do it because it’s bad  for business for people to hate your business.
They’re cross-pressured in that way. I think that  there’s nothing like healthcare and associated,
like getting your parents into a skilled nursing  facility type thing—it’s absolutely miserable.
COWEN: This is a small thing, but it bugs me  all the time. I’m on a purely private sector
website. I can’t blame the government at  all, and it turns out I already have an
account at the website. I try to register  as a guest, and it’s never that simple.
LOWREY: No.
COWEN: Why does this go wrong? Why is  this not fixed in a world with AI agents?
LOWREY: I’m convinced that white-collar  technology, labor-saving stuff,
I’m convinced it’s all Jevons paradoxical.  I think that basically anything that is
designed like email to make your life easier  will at some point make it worse. We’ve made
it so that it just multiplies the number  of tasks. The things that companies can
do to you multiplies. I do not want to use  passkeys. It feels like private companies are
just hell-bent on—I don’t want to know what  a passkey is—getting you to use them. It’s
absolutely nutty. The password managers, but then  you have to manage the manager. It’s all a lot.
COWEN: If I travel to Harvard and  maybe I bought a plane ticket for
$400 and I can get reimbursement,  that is hell. That’s one of the
worst private sector experiences I have  is learning a new software system to be
reimbursed for a small sum of money and  having to go through a whole rigmarole.
LOWREY: Yes, exactly. There’s some amount that
you just won’t do it because you value  your own time and your blood pressure,
right? It’s absolutely annoying. There  were these rules that used to make airlines
reimburse you if they bounced you off a plane.  That’s gone. Anything having to do with airlines,
and they’re like, “We’ve severely inconvenienced  you, so we’ve given you some miles,” or some
credit or something. This is the first book: Give  People Money. Give them cash. They like that.
COWEN: Now, government, virtually  by definition, operates at scale,
unless it’s, say, a small town. How long will  it be before AI agents are just built to do
almost all of this for us? You just say to your  agent, “Hey, fill out these benefits form,” and
then you go away, you go to sleep and it’s  done? Won’t that happen within five years?
LOWREY: I imagine so. The questions that I  have are, one, are the lower-income people,
who are the users of the most burdensome programs,
do they know about those agents? Do they  feel comfortable using them? I don’t know.
COWEN: Not now—
LOWREY: Not now.
COWEN: —but, say, within five years—
LOWREY: Yes, definitely.
COWEN: —if it’s just a pure gain.
LOWREY: The second thing is that a lot of it is  not really paperwork. It’s mandatory interviews,
it’s urine screens, it’s collecting  data that might be hard to collect,
and answering questions that an AI agent might  not be able to answer for you. For instance,
unlike other programs, jobless benefits are given  to the individual. It’s state and individual.
SNAP benefits depend on your  household. You, in some cases,
will have to say how you split up the cost  of staples with the people in your house.
It’s really hard because the government doesn’t  have a stable definition of what a household is,
and it could be very hard to say who is in your  household and how you’re splitting things up. I
think that AI will help with a lot of this. I was  skeptical, but the best civic technologist I know
thinks that it’ll help a lot—and he’s a guy who’s  been in the muck of this for a really long time,
and knows the technology part of it—he’s  convinced that AI will help. I don’t know.
COWEN: The AI can interview you and say, “Well,  please tell me these things. I’m going to need it
to answer the questions for your SNAP benefit.”  You intermediate through the AI, which is nicer,
friendlier, easier to deal with, and then it  deals with the nasty person in the government.
LOWREY: Yes, and very often, the government  will ask you a question in a way that some
lawyer wrote in some very legalistic fashion. I  think the AI is unusually good at saying, “Oh,
this is what they’re actually asking, and this is  what the general advice is for how to do that.”
COWEN: Now, very big picture question.  Fertility rates are low in the US,

it really depends on the quality of immigrants  we attract. If we have a welfare system where
it’s really hard to get benefits, don’t we, in  fact, attract a higher quality of immigrant,
more ambitious people and more self-sustaining,  than if benefits are just easy to get? Isn’t the
significance of that really quite large in  a future where native fertility is so low?
LOWREY: Why do you think it is that if  we have such a clunky system now we’ve

COWEN: Because people who want to come  just to get the benefits might say, “Oh,
in Europe, they’ll just hand me the money, give  me the free apartment, put me up in the hotel.”
LOWREY: I see what you mean.
COWEN: You come to the US, it’s a huge  pain. Maybe there’s a wisdom in that.
LOWREY: Yes, and you can come. My  understanding was that the welfare
magnet hypothesis didn’t pan out. It makes  some sense, but I think that the issue is,
can you actually get here and come  here is a big problem. Then you’re
barred from accessing the safety net  as an immigrant for long periods of it.
COWEN: Part. Much of it, yes. Not all of it.
LOWREY: Yes, not all of it. Your children,  especially if they’re born here, they have
access, so there’s that. In general, I  think the policies work well when they
have a direct goal rather than relying  on indirect mechanisms like these. If we
want to attract more and better immigrants,  why don’t we just create policies that will
get them to come here. Like, if you get your  PhD here, you automatically get a Green Card,
that kind of thing. I think that that would  lead a lot of immigrants to come back.
COWEN: The current system, it selects for  people having stamina, conscientiousness,
focus, drive, willing to put up with  indignities, and smart enough to get
through the systems that may not be in  their language. You could argue what
we have is those policies. I know plenty of  lazy PhDs. Most PhDs are lazy, I would say.
LOWREY: Really?
COWEN: I don’t want that to  be the standard. Of course,
they are. It’s become negative  selection, relative to IQ.
LOWREY: Huh. You’re looking for  entrepreneurial people with a
lot of get-up-and-go, people who can make  it through the maze that we have set up.
COWEN: More O-1s, and then somewhat reform H-1B,
and to have more of them, and  none of these crazy $100,000 fees.
LOWREY: If you’re thinking that the  H-1B and the O-1 is working well,
why not just make those much,  much, much bigger programs?
COWEN: Oh, of course, but keep the benefits  tough and stingy, or, in some cases, impossible,
which is not a time tax. If you know you  can’t get it, you don’t bother to apply,
but it’s like a time tax in the sense  that it keeps you away from the benefit.
LOWREY: Right. I just don’t think that you  should be creating chaos and taking people’s
time by making the actual administrative part  of it difficult. I think there’s always many
other ways to get the policy outcome that  you are searching for than larding the
government up. It means that the government  is wasting more money. Your overhead cost
is going to be higher. I know that immigration is  self-financing because we are applying these fees,
but nevertheless, I just think that  there’s better ways to go about it.
COWEN: Here’s a question from a reader,  which I’m paraphrasing: “Do you favor much
easier access to benefits, but randomized  harsh, credible punishments for offenders?
So you audit one in every 100, every 1,000  applications. If the person did something wrong,
you come down on them really hard. The time  tax mostly vanishes, but there’s still this
somewhat arbitrary punishment meted out  to some of the people who are frauds.”
LOWREY: I think you have to separate  out the issue of improper payments
from purposeful fraud. Improper payments are  a function of the complexity of this system.

who don’t own a computer for their monthly gross  income and also their net income over the past
six months, and that’s really hard to do, and  a million other little questions, the improper
payment rate would go down if the government were  doing more work and the rules were simpler. You

obscenely harsh punishment, though.  Why do you need the harsh punishment

COWEN: If you only audit one  in 5,000, people will think,
“Oh, I can get away with it.” The punishment  needs to really be harsh to scare them off.
LOWREY: Yes. I think you could just do more  reasonable audits. I don’t necessarily think

they knew that they put the wrong paperwork  in there. As a general point, I think that the
benefit fraud rate is quite low. I’m not concerned  that we’re losing too much money to fraud.
COWEN: Now, from 1990 to 2014, the number of  people on disability insurance increased by
about four times. Even though jobs got safer,  the number of people killed by their job went
down steadily. Does that not mean that  disability insurance should just be much
tougher to get? More bureaucracy, more  standards, more process, more whatever.
LOWREY: Yes. I think that there were some reasons  that more Americans became disabled. Population
