Yes, the caseload has gone up,  but recently it’s been going down,
so I don’t think that we’re worrying that it’s  just going up and up and up and up and up and up.
COWEN: Yes, it’s gone down a lot since 2014.
LOWREY: Gone down a lot, right?
COWEN: The job market got better, is part of it.
LOWREY: I worry that we are giving benefits  to people who are not disabled and do not need
them. I also worry that we are denying  benefits to people who actually do,
so I don’t know that I see a strong case for  making disability much more burdensome as opposed

so I don’t know that I see the case for  adding paperwork to it at this juncture.
COWEN: If I look at governments where  processes seem pretty straightforward,
they very often seem to have smaller  populations, say, below 20 million. Now,
I’m not sure what is causing what here, but what  do you think is the exact reason why a small

LOWREY: Yes, I think it’s, in some cases,  federalism. I think it’s homogeneity.

COWEN: Should the US have less federalism?
LOWREY: Yes.
COWEN: I’m not saying it’s practical  in the sense of getting support,

LOWREY: Absolutely.
COWEN: What would it be?
LOWREY: I think that there is the case for local  control of certain things; some things: policing,

LOWREY: No, but I don’t know about Staten Island.
COWEN: It’s big, right? I was  just going to ask about Staten

LOWREY: I think so. I guess that the people  of Staten Island should self-determine.
COWEN: What do you think they would do?
LOWREY: I don’t know. I don’t know. Actually,
I need to go over there and do some  surveying and knocking on doors.
COWEN: I haven’t been there in 20 years. Is  there Sri Lankan food? Is that the reason to go?
LOWREY: Yes, Sri Lankan food. I took the ferry.  The ferry costs $0. You go there and back,

I’ve not spent a lot of time on Staten Island.  I was reporting there a couple of years ago,

haven’t been in New York for long enough; I’m  not a New Yorker; I can’t set policy for New
York. Brooklyn feels like it should be part  of New York to me, now living in Brooklyn.
COWEN: There’s a theme recurring  through your book in a number of
different places that it’s too hard to vote.
LOWREY: Yes.
COWEN: Now, I’m of the view that  it should not be that easy to vote,
at least in the United States. What exactly is  the gain we get from having more people vote?
Given that, for instance, people didn’t  even know what the child tax credit was,
even if they were receiving it.  Don’t we just get better outcomes if,
say, only half the people vote, which of  course will skew toward the more educated?
LOWREY: I don’t think so.
COWEN: Why not?
LOWREY: I think that democracy is important for
reasons of principle that are  more important than policies.
COWEN: I’m all for democracy, right? There’s  no country where you can vote by just leaning
back on your sofa and screaming out whom  you favor. There’s some cost. You can set
the cost where you want. Americans today seem  fine with the costs being higher than in many
places. You make the costs lower, you get inferior  outcomes, including on the issues you care about.
LOWREY: I don’t know that I think  that that’s true. Do we know that?
COWEN: Maybe “no” is too strong a word,  but we know that more educated people
make better voting choices than  less educated people on average.
LOWREY: I think my view is  only principled. I don’t
care about outcomes. I think if you’re a  democracy, people should be able to vote.
COWEN: Oh, sure, they should  be able to, but how easily?
LOWREY: As easily as possible.
COWEN: You would, even in countries  with high voter participation rates,
subsidize voting, give everyone a  free ride, do whatever was necessary?
LOWREY: Yes, I think so. I think when  you look at countries with very high
voter participation rates, do you think  that they have worse outcomes, or do you
just think that their polities are different  such that you end up with different policies?
COWEN: The latter.
LOWREY: Voting is compulsory in some places.
COWEN: They tend to be better educated  at the lower end, for one thing.
LOWREY: Right. Then I think, again, you  want to do more education. You want to
make it easier for people to go to school. You  don’t want to make it hard for them to vote.
COWEN: I’m all for making school easier. Now, you  have an earlier book called Give People Money,
which is basically pro-UBI, to oversimplify a bit.
LOWREY: Indeed.
COWEN: There have been UBI  studies since then. How does
your current view differ from your earlier view?
LOWREY: I think that the studies have been  sobering, and, yes, I have updated my priors,
and I think that some of the ancillary benefits  that I thought we could see through cash haven’t
materialized, and I take that seriously. I think  that there is still a case for doing it, because
the point of giving people money is to merely  give them money so that they can buy things,
and I think that the case for that remains. I  think it is noncorrupted, that their lives don’t
improve as much as I would have thought, I think,  isn’t necessarily a case against the policy.
COWEN: There’s an argument that your earlier  argument is stronger than you thought. Say AI
truly is a big deal, and we all live to 100,  but day-to-day, we’re not really happier,
per se, because of AI. This, to me, is one  plausible scenario. I’m not sure it will happen,
but it could happen. Then the purpose  of UBI is not to make people happier,
but just to stop them from being  less happy due to instability.
LOWREY: Yes.
COWEN: The only benchmark is, can  UBI keep people where they were at,
on some dimensions, and they still get to  live to 100, which of course they want,
and then overall, it’s just a  way of making the system stable?
LOWREY: Yes, absolutely. When I wrote the  prior book, the AIs that were out were garbage,
and it was really not clear that they would  ever get to the place that people said that
they would get. I remember even when I  first moved out to the Bay Area in 2018,
you would talk to people who did AI work and  they seemed like religious zealots in some ways.
COWEN: Seemed like?
LOWREY: Yes, they’d be like, “No, I  promise it’s going to change everything;
I’ve seen inside the machine.”  I’d be like, “Okay, buddy. Sure,
great. The computer’s not really better,  and they aren’t really getting better,
and this is a time of really remarkably  little technological progress.” I was
very wrong about that and really found ChatGPT  remarkable when I got access to it, and I do.
I was extremely dismissive at the time of the  notion that AIs would necessitate UBI. I don’t
know that I would go so far as to say that  I think that we’ll need a UBI because of AI,
but I certainly think that we should  be starting to think about that kind of
policy if the improvements that we’re seeing  continue forward, and if there is a lot of
pressure on the white-collar workforce, which  I think we won’t know for a couple of years.
Yes, I think that if we see a situation  in which GDP is radically increasing,
productivity is increasing, and unemployment  is going up, that would be very strange,
and I think we would have to start  looking at UBI-type functions.
COWEN: Are raccoons evolving into pets?
LOWREY: No, they are not.
COWEN: Should they?
LOWREY: No.
COWEN: Should more things be  pets, or fewer things be pets?
LOWREY: Fewer things.
COWEN: No tigers?
LOWREY: No, I don’t think that you should be  able to have a nondomesticated animal as a
pet. This is one of my strongest-held  and probably least popular positions,
and that means that I do not think that you should  be able to have sugar gliders. I do not think you
should be able to have most types of fish. I  don’t think you should be able to keep birds.
COWEN: That would be federal or local governments  doing that? Getting back to our earlier question.
LOWREY: Federal.
COWEN: Federal?
LOWREY: Nondomesticated birds, I should  say. You can have chickens. Chickens
are domesticated, but tropical birds, I  don’t think you should be able to keep.
COWEN: Why are you visiting Namibia?
LOWREY: Ah, the Namib Desert. I’m very, very  excited to see petroglyphs. As a general point,
I organize a lot of my travel around  deserts and moss, to see those,
so I’m very, very excited. I’m very excited  for dark skies. I’ve been to South Africa,
but I haven’t traveled extensively in that region.
COWEN: You said moss, M-O-S-S?
LOWREY: Moss.
COWEN: Where is the best place  in the world to go see moss?
LOWREY: The Pacific Northwest, I think, is the  best moss that I have seen in the United States.
My understanding is that there are places in  Japan that have extraordinary moss. I have
only ever been to Tokyo. Have you been to mossy  places in Japan? You’re better traveled than I am.
COWEN: I think in retrospect, they seemed mossy,  but I wasn’t very aware of it at the time.
LOWREY: You’re not a moss traveler.  Have you been to the Sundarbans? I
don’t know how to say that. The  mangrove forest in Bangladesh?
COWEN: No, never been to Bangladesh  at all, I’m sorry to say.
LOWREY: I haven’t either,  and I very much want to go.
COWEN: Why do you like architectural brutalism?
LOWREY: Oh, I just find it visually  interesting and beautiful. I like to
feel tiny in front of buildings, and I like the  idea of creating warm spaces within imposing
structures that make you feel uncomfortable.  It’s like the jolie laide of architecture.
COWEN: My favorite brutalism is in former
communist countries. Do you  have a favorite brutalism?
LOWREY: Boston City Hall. It’s really ugly.
COWEN: Why are tattoos so popular  now, including with women?
LOWREY: For the same reason  we scribble on cave walls.
COWEN: One of those is your body, and  it’s still somewhat hard to reverse,
right? It can take 12 sessions  to get it off, and it hurts.
LOWREY: Yes, it’s reversible. I actually  think that the capacity to remove tattoos,
while wonderful for some people who have a tattoo  that is prohibiting them from getting employment,
reminding them of something painful, or, goodness  forbid, if you have hate speech or similar on your
body, I think it’s good that you can take the  tattoo off, but in general, I think that the
idea of having and then removing tattoos is  not good for tattoo culture. I have tattoos,
and I think that they’re a really nice reminder  of time and place. They’re permanent ephemera.
COWEN: You recently read a book called A  History of Christianity. Which one was it,
and what was interesting in the book to you?
LOWREY: This was A History of Christianity:  The First Three Thousand Years.
One of the things that really stuck with  me was that I, despite being Catholic,
had not entirely internalized that  Christians start off as a strange,
tiny Jewish sect of people that are found to  be often mentally unstable and deeply annoying.
COWEN: This book communicates that?
LOWREY: Indeed, that Judaism is not the  predominant mode of worship or culture
at the time, and Christianity, which then  comes to dominate so much of the globe,
starts off as an offshoot of that; of  people who are insisting that they are
seeing apparitions and people walking through  walls. It was a very, very, very good book.
COWEN: How essential do you view  Christianity to Western liberalism?
LOWREY: When you say “essential,” do you mean  “positive,” or do you just mean “influential”?
COWEN: Influential but positive: the notion that  Jesus Christ was an individual. It’s a story very
different from “might makes right.” We valorize  the victim. It easily translates into talk of
individual rights and liberties and constitutional  procedures, at least that has been argued.
LOWREY: Yes, I agree with that, but  I certainly don’t see Christianity as
essential to enlightenment or good governance  in any way, shape, or form. I do think that
it had that effect, but I don’t think that  it would be necessary in some other world.
COWEN: Not that many Christian  countries have achieved the same, right?
You could say Japan has for a while.
LOWREY: Yes, I was going to say Japan.
COWEN: Yes, that’s one.
LOWREY: South Korea?
COWEN: South Korea’s pretty Christian in terms  of actual belief. I’m not sure of the numbers.
LOWREY: Did it inform the  structure of government, though?
COWEN: I don’t know.
LOWREY: I don’t know. That’s an actual question;
I don’t know enough about it. I’ve been to  South Korea, but I don’t know that much.
COWEN: Other than Japan, I see very few examples.
LOWREY: Yes. I don’t know. I would  have to think about it more. Also,
there’s so much Christianity; it gets so  everywhere-d that I don’t know. I’m not sure.
COWEN: I tend to worry quite a bit, now  that we are genuinely less Christian,
that this will hurt the chances  of liberalism in our future.
LOWREY: I think that that might be right. I’m  not saying, when I’m talking about the church,
the political actor “the church,” which  obviously has a very checkered history,
but I do think that it was good that you had an  institution that was so predominant in people’s
lives, reminding them of the importance of  sin and of being a person of integrity and
caring for the neighbor. Although,  then again, the world, as it’s become
less Christian, it’s become safer, more  redistributive, so I’m not really sure.
COWEN: What do you think of Ross Douthat’s  famous comment? It’s something like, “Well,
if you don’t like the Christian right, wait till
you see the post-Christian right,”  which he said some while ago, right?
LOWREY: Yes. I think that’s completely accurate,
and I think that our most notable Christians  are not particularly Christian right now. Again,
as a Catholic, the notion of being yelled  at specifically by two successive popes,
as J. D. Vance has been, it’s tough  to imagine that. It’d be very painful.
COWEN: Other than facts about moss, what  is it you think you learn when you travel?
LOWREY: Oh, goodness. In some ways, I feel  like the emergence of a global monoculture,
this idea of it, I do think  that shows up especially in
urban places. I think that it is really,  really important to recognize your own
privilege and to see how other people live. I  think it’s important in the sense of trusting
that people know what they value and value  very, very, very different things than you do.
It slows time down, which is a big thing for  me. The time I spend traveling seems to go
20 times as slowly as an average  day in the office, and I really,
really like that telescoping effect, and I  look for nondrug ways for that to happen.
COWEN: Could you name a city that  you feel more or less successfully
rebels against the global monoculture,  but it’s not just a complete wreck?
You could say Lagos, but Lagos is  a complete wreck. A well-run city
that avoids the traps of many places, where  every coffee shop looks the same or whatever.
LOWREY: That’s a great question. A lot of  the traveling I do is for outdoors stuff,
and I do think that the global monoculture  and Instagram has been very terrible for that,
for opening beautiful places up to people who just  want to take photographs and leave. It’s really,
really awful. There, I understand it’s the “you’re  not in traffic, you are traffic” phenomenon,
but I really mean people who are desecrating  these places that are very fragile ecosystems
and where you do want to meter access, and  you do want people to, for instance, take
out their trash and understand what to do if you  encounter a wild animal and that kind of thing.
In terms of a city that feels  really, really wildly different,
I just think that there’s lots of  places I go that there’s no tourists,
and they’re wonderful for that. When I  report, even more so than being a tourist,
being a reporter is the best way to find  someplace because I’m always amazed by how
much people will tell you about their lives  and show you about their lives. You really
get to see life on the edge of Lake Victoria  or very close to the India-Bangladesh border.
Similarly, going to weddings abroad is  another way to do that, if you ever get
invited to a wedding. One of my favorite  weddings that I went to was in Pakistan,
which I never would have gone to  Pakistan, I think, without that,
or maybe I would have. It was a perfect  way to get a glimpse of Pakistani society.
COWEN: That, for me, is a case where  the private sector time tax is too high.
LOWREY: Yes. Oh, wow.
COWEN: If it were a half-day wedding, I would  go, but a three-day wedding in South Asia,
I’d just feel, no, I’ll be wanting to check  my email the whole time, and that’s rude.
LOWREY: Oh, yes. No, no. They really, really do  weddings well. I would also note that Pakistan,
I believe, has much heavier time taxes than we  do. There’s a lot of interesting thinking about
postcolonial states and paperwork burdens.
There’s a good book that I read about  Pakistan that I forget the exact title,
but it was about Pakistan’s issues with paperwork  and the transition from British rule to self-rule.
COWEN: Should friendships have  explicit time taxes? For instance,
people from the Soviet Union, they often expect  their friends to pick them up from the airport—
LOWREY: Oh, I love that. Yes.
COWEN: —even though that’s not a thing anymore.  You can just Uber, taxi. It doesn’t matter if
your income is high enough. It’s expected that  someone goes to pick you up. Is that good/bad?
LOWREY: Yes, there’s no inconvenience in  friendship if the point is to do things
and spend time together. I note that I think the  best way to make friends is not to make yourself
available for what other people need but to  ask for help. I remember one escalation of a
friendship that happened to me recently: My older  son had had a dental procedure in the morning,
and I needed to pick my younger son up  from school. My husband wasn’t around,
and no childcare was around, and my mom couldn’t  make it. The older son needed an adult to be with
him, and I couldn’t leave him alone, so I asked a  friend to come over and sit with this kid who had
just been given a large dose of ketamine for  20 minutes. I had a bunch of people say yes,
and one friend came over and sat with my son  in bed and looked at her phone for 20 minutes.
There is no inconvenience in friendship. People  like to be asked to do things, too, I think.
COWEN: That’s useful, right?  Say it’s not really useful,
that it’s just an ongoing act of  signaling to show you’re a true friend.
LOWREY: Oh, absolutely. Definitely.  It’s because I think that the point
is to spend time, certainly. Do you find  that there are social conventions that
you despise having to comply with in  your life but still have to do it?
COWEN: I don’t know. I don’t think I ever despise,
but there are various slight annoyances,  or I wish things were more efficient.
LOWREY: Yes. The one that I really struggle  with is that I have email and text and WhatsApp
and Signal and lots of other modes—Instagram  messages. I really, really despise having to
keep up with people on all of those forms  of communication. I think of texting as
being fundamentally asynchronous, and that you  shouldn’t have to socially respond to a text.
I only like socializing in person; I want to see  people, I want to be visually with them. I hate
all of the digital upkeep, and I’m really,  really bad at it, and it’s known among my
friends that I’m bad at this. Even my husband  is like, “You’re a terrible texter, and you’re
mean over text.” I’m like, “Well, I’m not trying  to be mean.” I text like a boomer, apparently.
COWEN: My slight gripe is there’s too  many networks, so I feel there should
be email and one system of texting. There’s  Signal, there’s WhatsApp, there’s iMessenger.
LOWREY: It’s too much.
COWEN: There’s other stuff.  There’s Twitter Direct Message.
LOWREY: Awful. I don’t do social media anymore,  so I don’t do Twitter anymore at all. I have
an Instagram account that I’m not on very  often. I don’t Facebook, I don’t Bluesky,
and I really appreciate the time that I’ve  gotten back from that. Particularly X, I think,
is a terrible mode of discourse, and I think  that it rewards unseemly emotions in people.
COWEN: Just to finish up with the last  question, I ask this of many of the guests,
but first, to mention your book  again, Annie Lowrey, The Time Tax:
How the Government Wastes Our Time—and How to  Fix It. What is it you wish to learn about next?
LOWREY: Oh, actually, I just got  two books about the Mexica people,
the Aztecs. I’d like to read those books and  then go see Aztec artifacts and structures.
COWEN: That’s a [Inga] Clendinnen book? A  lot of people have been reading that lately.
LOWREY: Yes, that was how I saw it. It was a  lot of people were reading it. Now I’m like,
“Who was it who recommended it?” I had  wanted to do more travel in Mexico,
so I got Fifth Sun, and then just  Aztecs, I think, is the other one,
which I’m excited to read. Actually, from  your podcast, I got the book on Vermeer,
which I’m excited—I know nothing about  him, and I’m very excited to read that.
COWEN: Great. Annie Lowrey, thank you very much.
LOWREY: Thank you.
